title: Shaking your head means yes
goal: Ask and deny correctly: put **ли** in the right place, stack negatives the way Bulgarian requires, and survive the head-shaking habit that reverses all your instincts.
bekal: forming yes/no questions with **ли** and moving their focus
using stacked negatives: **никой не, нищо не, никога не**
asking for confirmation when in doubt
reading Bulgarian head movements without misunderstanding

dialogs.title: Диалог — At the bus stop
dialogs.intro: Ani asks a man at the bus stop for help, and almost misunderstands him because of something that has nothing to do with language.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Excuse me, is this the stop for bus eighty-four?
lines.literal: excuse-me, here — (question) — is — stop-the — of — bus — eighty — and — four?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Really? But you're shaking your head…

lines.speaker: Мъж:
lines.id: Ah, you're a foreigner! Here, shaking your head means "yes".
lines.literal: ah, you — are — foreigner(f)! at — us — shaking-the — means — yes.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I'll never get used to it!

lines.speaker: Мъж:
lines.id: You will. Nobody gets used to it right away.
lines.literal: will — you-get-used. nobody — not — gets-used — immediately.

lines.speaker: Мъж:
lines.id: Only the head. The language is normal. Don't worry!
lines.literal: only — head-the. language-the — is — normal. not — yourself — worry!

notes: ⚠️ **This is no tourist tale: shaking your head really means "yes" in Bulgaria.** The side-to-side movement that means "no" almost everywhere else means agreement here. And "no" is shown by **tilting the chin up once**, often with a small *ts* click of the tongue. The exact opposite of your instincts.

**Why is it like this?** The most common explanation: under Ottoman rule, Bulgarians forced to give up their faith reversed their head movements so they could say "no" while appearing to agree. Historians doubt the story, but nobody has a better one — and every Bulgarian will tell it to you.

**What to do as a newcomer: trust the words, not the head.** For the first few months, listen for *да* and *не* and ignore the head movement. And for your own part, **say** your answer — never answer with a gesture alone.

**The most dangerous situation is a Bulgarian trying to help you.** Some people who deal with foreigners a lot reverse their gestures back on purpose to make things easier — and now you don't know which system is in use. The lifesaving line: **Да или не?** (*da EE-lee neh*).
**Наистина ли? means "really? is that so?"** and is one of the most useful ways to ask for confirmation without sounding as if you doubt the person.
**У нас literally means "at us" and means "in our country, where we live".** A very common pattern: *У нас е студено през зимата.* For the person you're talking to: *у вас* (where you live).
**Не се притеснявайте — "don't worry", formal.** To a friend: *Не се притеснявай.* The verb carries *се*, and in a prohibition *се* comes right after *не*.
**Езикът means "the language" and also "the tongue".** One word, two meanings — just like "mother tongue" in English. If someone complains *боли ме езикът*, they are talking about their tongue.

grammars.title: Ли — and how its position moves the question
body: Bulgarian does not change word order to ask a question. It slips **ли** in right after the word the question is about — and moving *ли* moves the whole point of the sentence.

head: Sentence
Say it
What is being asked
rows: Is it **you** who is going (not someone else)?

after: If nothing needs stressing, the default spot is **after the verb**: *Разбираш ли?* (Do you understand?), *Имате ли стая?* (Do you have a room?).
⚠️ *Ли* is never used if the sentence already has a question word. *Къде е спирката?* — no *ли*. Adding it is a classic beginner's mistake.
**Нали** is different and must not be mixed up: it goes at the **end** of the sentence and asks for agreement, like "right?" or "isn't it?". *Тук е спирката, нали?*

grammars.title: Stacked negatives — required, not wrong
body: In Bulgarian, a negative word **requires** the verb to be negated too. Dropping either one doesn't make the sentence shorter; it makes it wrong.

head: Word
Say it
English
Full sentence
English
rows: I have no money at all.

after: Compare standard English, which forbids stacking: "nobody doesn't know" means the opposite. In Bulgarian, the stacking is neutral and required. ⚠️ Your English instinct will keep dropping the *не*; practice until it feels natural.
With several negative words at once, all of them are used and there is still just one *не*: *Никой никога нищо не казва.* — Nobody ever says anything. Four negatives, one sentence, perfectly correct.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that **сигурен** follows the speaker's gender, like every adjective: a man says *не съм сигурен*, a woman *не съм сигурна*. This mistake stands out because the sentence is used so often.

sections.title: Head movements, and three other gestures

head: Gesture
In most countries it means
In Bulgaria it means
rows: Shaking the head side to side

blocks.text: The last row needs attention from the other side too: the *ts* click that sounds like an impatient "tsk" to you is completely neutral in Bulgaria and just means "no". Don't take offense.
The good news: two things never change and you can rely on them fully: **the word *да* always means yes, and the word *не* always means no.** The language never lies to you; only the head needs time.

blocks.title: Surviving the first week
items: **Say your answer.** Never answer with a head movement alone for the first few months; you will use the wrong system without noticing.
**When in doubt, ask.** *Да или не?* is never considered rude. Bulgarians know exactly why you are asking, and will usually chuckle and answer clearly.
**Watch the face, not the head.** The face of someone refusing and the face of someone agreeing look different anywhere in the world.

**Give yourself time.** Almost every foreigner living in Bulgaria says they only stopped misunderstanding after two or three months — and that after going home, they needed time again to get back to normal.

Complete with не in the right place. Remember the stacked negatives.

answers: Разбираш ли? — Той работи ли тук? — Имате ли стая? — Тя българка ли е? — Говорите ли английски? — Това спирката ли е?
Тук ли е спирката? — Никога няма да свикна. — Никой не свиква веднага. — Наистина ли? — Не се притеснявайте.
Нищо не разбирам. — Никой не знае. — Наистина ли? — Да или не? — Никога не закъснявам.
